posts.name: arenson9
posts.cooked:
Here's what I've learned about providing a live stream:

 

Option 1: Google+ Hangout

 

  • Created by going to G+ and clicking on 'Start a video party' in the lower right.
  • Can invite the public -- make it so that anyone with a G+ account can join the G+ Hangout.
  • The URL for the Hangout can be found and shared (via forums, Twitter, Facebook, G+, email, etc.)
  • Only ten people, however, can be in the Hangout at any one time.
  • People in the Hangout add their own audio/video to the Hangout, and can use a group chat interface inside the Hangout.
  • People outside the Hangout can not see or hear anything, as far as I can tell
  • One or more G+ posts or YouTube videos can be linked to the Hangout so that people outside the Hangout can comment and those comments would be seen by the creator of the Hangout. Comments could then be selectively displayed to the Hangout.

 

Option 2: YouTube Live Event, via Google+ Hangout on Air

  • If you have been blessed as worthy, there will be an option in YouTube's Video Manager to create a Live Event
  • Creating the Live Event results in both a YouTube video and a Google+ Hangout.
  • The G+ Hangout is like the above in option 1 except that you can not invite large groups, much less the public, to it.
  • The YouTube video shows the G+ Hangout with a several minute delay.

 

Option 3: YouTube Live Event, via custom encoder

  • Haven't explored this much. Apparently you can download free software to encode and broadcast your video stream without going through Google+ Hangout on Air, but I don't see how doing so is going to lead to any more interactivity between viewers of the stream and people delivering the stream.

 

Having thought about this a bit, I see the following potential goals:

  1. Allow remote people to see the fun that's happening
  2. Allow remote people to post messages that will be seen by other remote people and by the Vengeance party
  3. Allow remote people to videoconference (share their own audio/video) with the Vengenace party
  4. Allow remote people to play games with partygoers

 

If we just want to do #1 (see the party) option #2 (YouTube Live Event) works. I don't see a way to do #2 (share messages) with either option above. We can do #3 (videoconference) for up to nine people with either option. For #4, either option would be fine.

 

My current thought is to split the ideas of people playing the game from people watching/interacting with the party. We already know how to have games online. That's basically option #1. We could do that with a dedicated table and computer for a given game. For everything else, perhaps we could set up a station with a camera with a wide view of the party, or even someone with a tablet walking around.

 

My questions for people who will be remote:

  1. Do you want to be able to play games w/ people at the party?
  2. What else might you want -- see the party, post messages, videoconference in, something else?
  3. Anybody have good ideas about how to make this happen?

It's actually unclear to me whether or not we are allowed to share the Easter Egg stuff we saw. 

It also feels a little weird talking about the Vengeance cards or box. We went to a release party, so it's released, but the Kickstarter rewards haven't been sent out yet. I'm pretty sure it is ok to talk about it. Just feels a little weird.

 

The party was fun. It was very informal. There was no schedule beyond start and stop times. it started off with people trickling in, picking up games, and in some cases introducing themselves to people they'd only ever interacted w/ online. Paul was often at a table helping people pick up their games or packing Kickstarter boxes, often with Jodie. Christiopher and Adam were circulating. There were half a dozen tables set up in the front of the warehouse that filled up with people playing Vengeance. There were also games going on everywhere they could be fit into the office area -- the conference room, an unused office, the front lobby, and a wide hallway.I'm pretty sure we had ten simultaneous games while also having other people socializing, so I'm guessing the attendance was round 50-60 people.

All the office spaces were open and people wandered in and out. Paul has an office with some beautiful Lord of the Rings art and weapons mounted on the wall. The spare office has a bookshelf filled with fantasy miniatures. Christopher and Adam share an office with their desks facing each other. On one end Adam had hung eight gorgeous, framed comic pages. It wasn't Sentinels. I didn't recognize it. I don't _think_ it was his art work, but am not sure. There was also a whiteboard in their shared office. It already had a large line drawing of Baron Blade on it. Adam drew Legacy on the other side, while I held up my laptop so the people who were interacting via G+ could see him in action.

Reckless showed up with his perler (sp?) ... uh ... artwork? (not sure how to describe these). These are individually great, but even more impressive as a collection. Evan and his friends were doing various film/interview things and Evan coralled the forumites for a photo. Who knows what I may have missed, as well. You certainly couldn't see everything that was going on from a single vantage point.

Towards five, Christopher announced it was time for dinner. Those who had the time and inclination (~30) regrouped at a nearby Indian restaurant for a tasty buffet. Our carload of people left before 7, perhaps a bit earlier than we might have otherwise, in order to try to outrun the freezing rain that was overtaking the area.

I spoke to people who'd traveled from Fayetteville, Kansas City, Chicago, Indianapolis, and Columbus. And Brocolli. Who's from Texas, but he flies enough that maybe it wasn't very onerous to take one more trip. I'm not sure where else people might have travelled from.

It was pretty low key, but quite nice.
